meta.description: Yes — George H.W. Bush really said it, at the 1988 Republican convention on Aug 18. Speechwriter Peggy Noonan crafted the line. Here is the documented source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Read my lips: no new taxes'?
meta.ogDescription: George H.W. Bush said it in his 1988 RNC acceptance speech (Aug 18, New Orleans). Peggy Noonan wrote the line. The verified source and full passage.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Bush delivered the line in his acceptance speech at the 1988 Republican National Convention in New Orleans on 18 August 1988. The wording was crafted by speechwriter Peggy Noonan, but Bush himself spoke it — making this one of the few high-profile political one-liners whose source is fully documented rather than apocryphal.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: And the Congress will push me to raise taxes, and I’ll say no, and they’ll push, and I’ll say no, and they’ll push again, and I’ll say to them: ‘Read my lips: no new taxes.’
trail: The documented record places the line in Bush’s acceptance speech at the 1988 Republican National Convention in New Orleans on 18 August 1988.
The wording was written by speechwriter Peggy Noonan — so the phrasing is hers, though Bush is the one who spoke it aloud on national television.
The expression “read my lips” was already a colloquial idiom before 1988; Bush’s speech is what fixed it in political memory.
source.excerptNote: The famous phrase is the climax of a longer passage in which Bush dramatizes refusing Congress.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of George H.W. Bush and speechwriter Peggy Noonan
source.rightsNote: The acceptance speech containing this line was first delivered and published in 1988, well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so the speech text is in copyright. (A six-word slogan on its own is generally too short for copyright, but the surrounding speech — drafted by Peggy Noonan — is protected.)

author.name: George H.W. Bush
author.heading: About George H.W. Bush
author.bio: George Herbert Walker Bush served as the 41st President of the United States after a long career as a congressman, U.N. ambassador, CIA director, and Ronald Reagan’s vice president. His 1988 pledge became the defining line of his campaign — and, after he agreed to a 1990 budget deal that raised taxes, a symbol of the broken promise that Bill Clinton used against him in 1992. Bush lost his re-election bid, making him a one-term president.

misattribution.heading: The nuance
misattribution.intro: Unlike most quotes pinned on famous politicians, this one is genuinely Bush’s — he really said it. The honest caveats are about authorship and origin, not attribution.

items.why: The line was written by campaign speechwriter Peggy Noonan, not composed by Bush himself. Bush delivered it, so crediting the quote to him is correct — but the memorable phrasing is Noonan’s craft.
“Read my lips” was already an everyday colloquial expression meaning ‘listen closely, I mean it.’ Bush’s speech didn’t invent the phrase — it welded it to a tax pledge.

misattribution.truthLine: George H.W. Bush did say “Read my lips: no new taxes” — on 18 August 1988, in a speech written by Peggy Noonan. The attribution is real; only the authorship of the phrasing is shared.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The pledge helped Bush win the presidency in 1988 by drawing a sharp anti-tax contrast with his Democratic opponent. But in 1990, facing a budget deal with a Democratic Congress, Bush agreed to tax increases — breaking the promise in the most quotable possible terms.
The reversal handed opponents a ready-made attack. Bill Clinton hammered it in 1992, and the broken pledge is widely cited as a key reason Bush became a one-term president.
context.pull: The line that helped elect him in 1988 helped defeat him in 1992.
